Jeffery Daniels }} {{New Netherland}} '''Hempstead''' is a [[village (New York)|village]] located in the [[Hempstead, New York|Town of Hempstead]] in [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]], on [[Long Island]], in [[New York (state)|New York]], United States. The population was 59,169 at the time of the 2020 census, making it the most populous village in New York.{{Cite web |title=Explore Census Data |url=https://data.census.gov/all?q=Hempstead+village,+New+York |access-date=January 30, 2023 |website=data.census.gov}} The '''Incorporated Village of Hempstead''' is the site of the seventeenth-century "town spot" from which English and Dutch settlers developed the Town of Hempstead, the [[North Hempstead, New York|Town of North Hempstead]], and ultimately what would become Nassau County centuries later. It is the largest community by population in both the Town of Hempstead and Nassau County. [[Hofstra University]] is partially located within the village.{{Cite web |title=Hofstra University {{!}} Long Island, New York |url=https://www.hofstra.edu/ |access-date=September 1, 2020 |website=www.hofstra.edu}} == History == ===Foundation=== [[Image:TownOfHempsteadHall.jpg|thumb|The Town of Hempstead's old Town Hall, located at the corner of Front and Washington streets]] The land on which the Village of Hempstead stands was under Dutch control from the early 1620s. In the fall of 1643, two followers of the Presbyterian minister Richard Denton, Robert Fordham and John Carman, crossed [[Long Island Sound]] by rowboat to negotiate with the local Native Americans for a tract of land upon which to establish a new community. Representatives of the [[Marsapeague]] (Massapequa), [[Mericock]] (Merrick), [[Matinecock]] and [[Rekowake]] (Rockaway) tribes met with the two men at a site slightly west of the current Denton Green in Hempstead Village. Tackapousha, who was the [[sachem]] (chief spokesman) of the Marsapeague, was the acknowledged spokesman for conducting the transaction.{{cite web|url=http://longislandgenealogy.com/hempstead.html|title=History of Hempstead Village|publisher=Long Island Genealogy (James. B. York - Municipal Historian of Inc. Village of Hempstead)|year=1998|access-date= August 18, 2007}} The Indians sold approximately 64,000 acres (260 km2), the present day towns of [[Hempstead, New York|Hempstead]] and [[North Hempstead, New York|North Hempstead]], for an unknown quantity of items; a 1657 revisit of this agreement names large and small cattle, stockings, wampum, hatchets, knives, trading cloth, powder, and lead given as payment by the English.Schultz, Bernice. Colonial Hempstead. Lynbrook, New York: The Review-Star Press, 1937, pp. 11–12, 28. Some items may have been valuable to the Native Americans in terms of the contemporary markets for European "trinkets," which may have held symbolic and spiritual importance to Native America peoples in the Northeast.{{cite journal|last1=Hammell|first1=George R.|title=Strawberries, Floating Islands, and Rabbit Captains: Mythical Realities and European Contact in the Northeast During the 16th and 17th Centuries|journal=Journal of Canadian Studies|date=Feb 1987|volume=21}} In the spring of 1644, thirty to forty families left [[Stamford, Connecticut]], crossed Long Island Sound, landed in [[Roslyn, New York|Hempstead Harbor]] and eventually made their way to the present site of the village of Hempstead where they began their English settlement within Dutch-controlled [[New Netherland settlements|New Netherland]]. The settling of Hempstead marked the beginnings of the oldest English settlement in what is now Nassau County. Subsequent trips across the Sound brought more settlers who prepared a fort here for their mutual protection. These original Hempstead settlers were [[Puritan]]s in search of a place where they could more freely express their particular brand of [[Protestantism]]. They established a Presbyterian church that is the oldest continually active Presbyterian congregation in the nation. In 1843, Benjamin F. Thompson wrote and published a history of the village, and an account of contemporary Hempstead Village. Thompson reported that there were 200 dwellings, and 1,400 residents; that the village was connected to [[New York City]] by a [[Hempstead Turnpike|turnpike]] and a railroad; that it had dry soil, excellent water, and pure air; and that it was the principal place of mercantile, and mechanical business, in the county. The village of Hempstead was incorporated on May 6, 1853, becoming the first community in [[Queens|Queens County]] (Nassau County did not exist as a separate county until 1899) to do so. ===Rise=== As the years passed, the population of Hempstead increased, as did its importance and prestige. Between 1703 and 1705, the newly formed [[St. George's Episcopal Church (Hempstead)|St. George's Church]] received a silver communion service from [[England]]'s [[Anne, Queen of Great Britain|Queen Anne]]. During the [[American Revolution]], Hempstead was a center of [[Loyalist (American Revolution)|British sympathizers]].[[Natalie Naylor|Naylor, Natalie A.]] (2005). "[https://books.google.com/books?id=tmHEm5ohoCUC&pg=PA707 Hempstead (Town)]". ''The Encyclopedia of New York State''. Syracuse, NY: Syracuse University Press. {{ISBN|9780815608080}}. p. 707. The British attempted to occupy Hempstead after the [[Battle of Long Island]], and used St. George's as a headquarters as well as a place to worship. Judge [[Thomas Jones (historian)|Thomas Jones]] faulted a lax peace treaty for forcing the evacuation of the loyalists.{{citation needed|date=January 2017}} In the 19th century, Hempstead became increasingly important as a trading center for [[Long Island]]. In 1853, it became the first self-governing incorporated village in the Town of Hempstead. Many prominent families such as the [[Vanderbilt family|Vanderbilts]] and the [[August Belmont|Belmonts]] built homes here, making Hempstead a center of Long Island society. Hempstead merchants established routes out to outlying farms and served as a distribution point for many firms. Wagons would leave Hempstead loaded with tobacco, candy, and cigarettes and return in a week to restock. Bakeries covered routes from [[Baldwin, Nassau County, New York|Baldwin]] to [[Far Rockaway, Queens|Far Rockaway]] daily. Butchers ran routes to [[Seaford, New York|Seaford]], [[Elmont, New York|Elmont]], [[Valley Stream, New York|Valley Stream]], [[Wantagh, New York|Wantagh]], [[East Meadow, New York|East Meadow]], [[Creedmoor Psychiatric Center|Creedmoor]], [[East Rockaway, New York|East Rockaway]] and [[Christian Hook, New York|Christian Hook]]. Drugs, medicines, perfumes, extracts, aprons, children's coats and dresses and men's clothes were peddled about the country by Hempstead merchants. People came from all sections of Queens to purchase stoves, and there were few places outside Hempstead where stoves could be purchased. Hempstead was the shopping center for Nassau County and the eastern portion of Queens – those settlements within that county east of Jamaica before 1899, when they separated to form Nassau County, following the creation of the [[City of Greater New York]] in 1898. Hempstead has historically been the center of commercial activity for the eastern counties of Long Island. In Nassau County, all major county roads emanate from this village. During the 18th and 19th centuries, all stagecoaches en route to [[Suffolk County, New York|eastern Long Island]] from Brooklyn passed through Hempstead. Today, seventeen bus routes and three interstate buses leave from the village every day. In addition, the [[Hempstead Branch]] of the [[Long Island Rail Road]] has its terminal here. At one time, there were three railroad companies with terminals within the village."The Creation of Nassau County"- Published 1960, by the Nassau County Historical Museum In March 1898, Camp Black was formed on the [[Hempstead Plains]] (roughly the shared location of Hempstead and [[Garden City, New York|Garden City]]), in support of the impending [[Spanish–American War]]. Camp Black was bounded on the north by [[Old Country Road]], on the west by Clinton Road, and on the south by the [[Central Branch (Long Island Rail Road)|Central Line]] rail. Camp Black was opened on April 29, 1898, as a training facility and a point of embarkation for troops.{{cite web |url=http://longislandgenealogy.com/CampBlack/CampBlack.html |title=Camp Black – Garden City, Hemstead Plains 1898 |publisher=Long Island Genealogy |access-date=August 18, 2007}} Early Long Islanders made their living in agriculture or from the sea. Hempstead, with its central location, became the marketplace for the outlying rural farming communities. It was a natural progression, as the surrounding areas developed from small farms into today's [[suburbia]], that Hempstead Village would remain as the marketplace. [[Chain store|Chain]] [[department stores]], such as [[Arnold Constable & Company|Arnold Constable]] and [[Abraham & Straus]], called Hempstead home for many years. Hempstead's Abraham & Straus was the largest grossing suburban department store in the country during the late 1960s. Hempstead was Nassau's retail center during the 1940s through the 1960s. === Decline === The advent of regional [[shopping mall]]s such as the one at nearby [[Roosevelt Field Mall|Roosevelt Field]], the demise of nearby [[Mitchel Air Force Base]] in 1961 as well as the changing [[demographics]] put the retail trade in the village into a downward spiral that it was unable to recover from during the recessions of the 1970s and 1980s. A plethora of businesses left the village in the 1980s and early 1990s, including Abraham & Straus.{{Cite news |last=McQuiston |first=John T. |date=1992-06-19 |title=A & S in Hempstead Closing After 40 Years |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/06/19/nyregion/a-s-in-hempstead-closing-after-40-years.html |access-date=2026-06-15 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} ===Rebound and modern history=== [[Image:Village of Hempstead.jpg|thumb| Downtown Hempstead, as seen from eastbound [[New York State Route 24|Fulton Street (NY 24)]]]] {{More citations needed|date=January 2019}} In the course of the 1990s the village saw redevelopment as a government center as well as business center.{{Cite web|title=From the Desk of Mayor John Ryan - Week of October 1, 2018|url=https://www.villageofhempstead.org/DocumentCenter/View/13323/From-The-Desk-of-Mayor-Don-Ryan-week-of-10118-BOH-James-Garner|access-date=September 1, 2020|website=Village of Hempstead, NY}}{{Cite web|last=Asbury|first=John|date=September 29, 2018|title=Street named for LI's first African-American mayor|url=https://www.newsday.com/long-island/nassau/hempstead-village-325th-anniversary-o92781|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930010941/https://www.newsday.com/long-island/nassau/hempstead-village-325th-anniversary-1.21313484|url-status=live|archive-date=September 30, 2018|access-date=September 1, 2020|website=Newsday|language=en}} There are more government employees from all levels of government in the village than there are in [[Mineola, New York|Mineola]], the county seat. According to James York, the municipal historian, writing in 1998, the population during the day might rise to nearly 200,000, from a normal census of 50,000. Retailers' interest in the village was rekindled, due to the aggressive revitalization efforts of former Mayor [[James Garner (politician)|James Garner]], who served from 1989 to 2005, and former Community Development Agency Commissioner, Glen Spiritis, who served under Garner's administration. Specifically, two large tracts of retail property have recently undergone redevelopment. The former {{convert|8.8|acre|m2|adj=on}} [[Times Square Stores|Times Squares Stores (TSS)]] property on [[Peninsula Boulevard]] and Franklin Street has been redeveloped as Hempstead Village Commons, a {{convert|100000|sqft|m2|adj=on}} retail center.{{Citation needed|date=September 2020}} The former Abraham & Straus department store on {{convert|17|acre|m2}} was eventually also demolished; it was replaced by a large retail development and many other smaller establishments.{{Citation needed|date=September 2020}} A considerable infusion of state and federal funding, as well as private investment, have enabled the replacement of blighted storefronts, complete commercial building rehabilitations and the development of affordable housing for the local population. In 1989, Hempstead residents elected [[James Garner (politician)|James A. Garner]] as their mayor. He was the first Black or African-American mayor ever elected to office on Long Island, and he served for four consecutive terms. Subsequently, Wayne Hall – a former Village of Hempstead trustee who is also African American – served as mayor for three terms, from 2005 to 2017.{{Cite web|last=Cassese|first=Sid|date=August 31, 2016|title=LI mayor on the mend after kidney transplant|url=https://www.newsday.com/long-island/nassau/wayne-hall-sr-hempstead-mayor-home-after-kidney-transplant-s96009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160901141814/http://www.newsday.com/long-island/nassau/wayne-hall-sr-hempstead-mayor-home-after-kidney-transplant-1.12244358|url-status=live|archive-date=September 1, 2016|access-date=September 1, 2020|website=Newsday|language=en}}{{cite news |last1=Dazio |first1=Stefanie |last2=Asbury |first2=John |date=March 22, 2017 |url=https://www.newsday.com/long-island/politics/hempstead-village-gets-new-mayor-as-don-ryan-defeats-wayne-hall-w93159 |title=Hempstead Village gets new mayor as Don Ryan defeats Wayne Hall |work=Newsday |access-date=June 3, 2017}} The first African-American male judge, Lance Clarke, was elected in 2001. Cynthia Diaz-Wilson was the first female justice in the Village of Hempstead and first African American village justice in the state of New York.{{citation needed|date = June 2021}} The replacement of the 1913 [[Long Island Rail Road]] [[Hempstead (LIRR station)|Hempstead Terminal]] with a modern facility was completed in 2002,{{cite news | title = LIRR Hempstead Station Hub Reconstruction Work Marked by Dedication Ceremony | work = Three Village Times | date = March 19, 1999 | url = http://www.antonnews.com/threevillagetimes/1999/03/19/news/railroad.html | access-date = January 30, 2019 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080906222113/http://www.antonnews.com/threevillagetimes/1999/03/19/news/railroad.html | archive-date = September 6, 2008 }} and a four-story, 112-unit building for senior housing – with retail on the ground level – was completed at Main and West Columbia Streets four years prior, in January 1998. 32 units of affordable townhouses, known as Patterson Mews – located at Henry Street and Baldwin Road – was completed and fully occupied in 1997.{{Citation needed|date=September 2020}} In recent years, there has been concern regarding ongoing gang activity in certain neighborhoods, notably the "Heights", in addition to the issue of illegal rentals (homes/apartments that are illegally-subdivided by slumlords) and racial steering.{{Cite web|last=Rivera|first=Laura|date=February 3, 2009|title=Hempstead Village proposes illegal-rental crackdown|url=https://www.newsday.com/long-island/nassau/hempstead-village-proposes-illegal-rental-crackdown-1.890080|access-date=September 1, 2020|website=Newsday|url-status=dead|language=en|archive-date=January 24, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210124164310/https://www.newsday.com/long-island/nassau/hempstead-village-proposes-illegal-rental-crackdown-1.890080}} Hempstead was also one of the first Long Island communities to contend with the [[Salvadoran]] gang, [[MS-13]].{{Cite web|last=Murphy|first=Bridget|title=Two alleged MS-13 members convicted of murder|url=https://www.newsday.com/long-island/crime/ms13-killings-hempstead-1.34953492|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190812215851/https://www.newsday.com/long-island/crime/ms13-killings-hempstead-1.34953492|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 12, 2019|date=August 12, 2019|access-date=September 1, 2020|website=Newsday|language=en}} The continual intra-violence this gang has exhibited has led to the formation of their arch-rivals, "SWP" or "Salvadorans with Pride". These issues have contributed to Hempstead's high crime rate as compared to other communities in the area. A 2019 investigation by ''[[Newsday]]'' revealed widespread racial discrimination by real estate agents on Long Island, including within Hempstead.{{Cite web|last=Carrozzo|first=Anthony|date=November 17, 2019|title=Undercover investigation reveals evidence of unequal treatment by real estate agents|url=https://projects.newsday.com/long-island/real-estate-agents-investigation/|access-date=September 1, 2020|website=Newsday|language=en-US}} === Etymology === Hempstead may have been named after [[Hemel Hempstead]] in the [[England|English]] county of [[Hertfordshire]], where village founder John Carman was born. Another theory regarding the origin of the village's name is that it is derived from the town of [[Heemstede]] in the [[Netherlands]], as this was an area from which many Dutch settlers of New Netherland originated. In 1664, the new settlement adopted the [[The Duke's Laws|Duke's Laws]], an austere set of laws that became the basis upon which the laws of many colonies were to be founded. For a time, Hempstead became known as "Old Blue," as a result of the [[blue law]]s. ==Geography== [[File:Hempstead-village-ny-map.gif|thumb|U.S. census map of Hempstead]] According to the [[United States Census Bureau]], the village has a total area of 3.7 square miles (9.5 km2), all land.{{cite web|url=https://www.census.gov/geographies/reference-files/time-series/geo/gazetteer-files.html|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=April 23, 2011|date=February 12, 2011|title=US Gazetteer files: 2010, 2000, and 1990}} The Village of Hempstead differs from the majority of Nassau County as its population density is about 15,000 people per square mile—almost four times that of its neighbor on its northern border, [[Garden City, New York|Garden City]]. === Climate ===
According to the [[Köppen climate classification]], Hempstead has a [[Humid subtropical climate]] (type Cfa) with cool, wet winters and hot, humid summers.{{Cite web |title=Interactive United States |'''100.00%''' |} === 2010 census === As of the [[census]] of 2010, there were 53,891 people, 15,234 households, and 10,945 families residing in the village. The racial makeup of the village was 21.9% [[White (U.S. census)|White]], 44.2% [[Hispanic (U.S. census)|Hispanic]], 48.3% [[African American (U.S. census)|Black]] or [[Race (United States census)|African American]], 0.6% [[Native American (U.S. census)|Native American]], 1.4% [[Asian (U.S. census)|Asian]], 0.0% [[Pacific Islander (U.S. census)|Pacific Islander]], 22.8% from [[Race (United States census)|other races]], and 5.0% from two or more races. There were 16,034 households, out of which 38.7% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 39.0% were [[Marriage|married couples]] living together, 27.0% had a female householder with no husband present, and 26.4% were non-families. 20.8% of all households were made up of individuals, and 6.7% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 3.41 and the average family size was 3.76.{{cite web |title=U.S. Census website |url=https://www.census.gov |access-date=January 31, 2008 |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]}} In the village, the population was spread out, with 26.2% under the age of 18, 16.3% from 18 to 24, 31.4% from 25 to 44, 17.5% from 45 to 64, and 8.5% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 29 years. For every 100 females, there were 91.6 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 86.4 males. The [[median income]] for a household in the village was $45,234 and the median income for a family was $46,675. Males had a median income of $29,493 versus $27,507 for females. The [[per capita income]] for the village was $15,735. About 14.4% of families and 17.7% of the population were below the [[poverty line]], including 20.7% of those under age 18 and 16.9% of those age 65 or over. ==Government== As of August 2022, the Mayor of Hempstead is Waylyn Hobbs, Jr, the Deputy Mayor is Jeffery Daniels, and the Village Trustees are Kevin Boone, [[Noah Burroughs]], Jeffery Daniels, and Clariona D. Griffith.{{Cite web |title=Government {{!}} Hempstead, NY |url=https://www.villageofhempstead.org/27/Government |access-date=August 19, 2022 |website=www.villageofhempstead.org}}{{Cite web |title=Village Trustees {{!}} Hempstead, NY |url=https://www.villageofhempstead.org/295/Village-Trustees |access-date=August 19, 2022 |website=www.villageofhempstead.org}} In the 2024 U.S. presidential election, the majority of Hempstead voters voted for [[Kamala D. Harris]] ([[Democratic Party (United States)|D]]).{{Cite web |last=Welch |first=Will |date=November 8, 2017 |title=How Long Island Voted |url=https://projects.newsday.com/long-island/how-long-island-voted/?election=2016%20General&position=U.S.%20President®ion=United%20States |access-date=June 23, 2021 |website=Newsday}}{{Cite web |last=LaRocco |first=Paul |date=2024-11-12 |title=Map: How Long Island voted for president in Harris-Trump race |url=https://www.newsday.com/long-island/politics/elections/trump-harris-election-results-uuvmm1tu |access-date=2024-11-12 |website=Newsday |language=en}} ==Education== [[File:Hofstra University, Student Center.jpg|thumb|The Mack Student Center at [[Hofstra University]], partially located within the village]] === Primary and secondary education === The community is served by the [[Hempstead Union Free School District]].{{Cite web |title=Long Island Zoning Atlas |url=http://www.longislandindexmaps.org/ |access-date=August 19, 2022 |website=www.longislandindexmaps.org}} Students attend Alverta B. Gray-Schultz Middle School and [[Hempstead High School (New York)|Hempstead High School]] for their secondary years of K-12 education.{{Cite web |title=Hempstead Union Free School District / Home |url=https://www.hempsteadschools.org/ |access-date=September 1, 2020 |website=Hempstead UFSD |language=en}} There is one private high school in Hempstead: [[Sacred Heart Academy (New York)|Sacred Heart Academy]] – a private, all-girls [[Catholic school]].{{Cite web |title=Explore Sacred Heart Academy |url=https://www.niche.com/k12/sacred-heart-academy-hempstead-ny/ |access-date=September 1, 2020 |website=Niche |language=en}} There are two charter schools located within the village: the Academy Charter School and Evergreen Charter School. === Higher education === [[Hofstra University]]'s campus is partially located within the Village of Hempstead; it is split between Hempstead and its unincorporated neighbor, [[Uniondale, New York|Uniondale]]. ==Transportation== The [[Rosa Parks Hempstead Transit Center]] is one of the largest hubs in [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]].{{Cite web|title=Rosa Parks Hempstead Transit Center|url=https://www.newsday.com/entertainment/long-island-venues/rosa-parks-hempstead-transit-center-1.1964219|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161104235738/http://www.newsday.com/entertainment/long-island-venues/rosa-parks-hempstead-transit-center-1.1964219|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 4, 2016|access-date=September 1, 2020|website=Newsday|language=en}} It serves as the terminus of the [[Long Island Rail Road]]'s [[Hempstead Branch]], and is served by a number of [[Nassau Inter-County Express]] routes.{{Cite web|title=Nassau Inter-County Express - Maps and Schedules|url=https://www.nicebus.com/Tools/Maps-and-Schedules|access-date=September 1, 2020|website=www.nicebus.com}} [[File:Hempstead Transit Center.jpg|thumb|The bus terminal at the [[Rosa Parks Hempstead Transit Center]]]] [[File:Hempstead LIRR SW Corner.jpg|thumb|The [[Long Island Rail Road|LIRR]] terminal at the [[Rosa Parks Hempstead Transit Center]]]] {| class="wikitable" style="font-size: 100%;" |+List of Nassau Inter-County Express bus routes serving Hempstead: | style="background:orange;
